Dorotheus of Tyre: A Saintly Figure in the Early Christian Era

Dorotheus of Tyre (fl. 2nd century CE) was a bishop of the early Christian church, traditionally credited with an Acts of the Seventy Apostles, who were sent out according to the Gospel of Luke 10:1.

Born in Tyre, a major port city in the Roman province of Phoenicia, Dorotheus rose to prominence as a leader in the early Christian community. He played a significant role in the spread of Christianity throughout the Mediterranean world, particularly during the reign of Emperor Constantine (306-337 CE).

The Acts of the Seventy Apostles, attributed to Dorotheus, describe the missionary journeys of seventy disciples sent out by Jesus Christ himself. This work is considered one of the most important sources for understanding the early Christian church and its practices.

Dorotheus' legacy extends beyond his writings, as he is remembered as a patron saint of sailors and traders. His feast day, celebrated on May 26th, has become an important holiday in many Christian traditions.

The influence of Dorotheus can still be felt today, with many churches and institutions around the world tracing their roots back to this early Christian leader.
